title: Elastic GPU routing and KV segmentation (WIP)
content:
Summary:

This is a working doc that explores an alternative multi-GPU serving architecture focused on two coordinated mechanisms: 1) elastic GPU routing (a lightweight, request-level steering layer that selects the best GPU or GPU-group for a request) and 2) KV segmentation (a consistent-segmentation scheme for the KV cache that reduces cross-GPU KV traffic and enables fast rebalancing). The goal is to reduce per-token latency variance and NCCL pressure for large context chat workloads while maintaining high throughput.

Context and motivation:
- Current approaches we've evaluated: large contiguous KV shards pinned to GPUs, slice-and-stitch, and aggressive NCCL allreduce/collective strategies. These can work, but we observe:
  - Heavy NCCL churn when many short requests hit different token prefixes (small batches, many routes).
  - Uneven KV hotness: a small fraction of prompts access a large portion of the KV working set; static shard placement causes cross-GPU fetches and latency spikes.
  - Rollout friction when scaling up/down GPUs — large re-sharding windows or expensive full-state copy.

Design goals (ranked):
1) Minimize 99th percentile token latency for typical chat workloads (seq len 512–2048).
2) Keep NCCL collective activity proportional to the useful work (avoid global allreduce per token when possible).
3) Support elastic cluster size changes with minimal blocking and low bandwidth migration.
4) Preserve model correctness and deterministic KV reads for a given model version.
5) Integrate with existing routing/fallback stack (hosted/dedicated/private).

High-level idea:
- Separate routing (where to run attention/FFN ops) from KV ownership. Each GPU advertises: compute capacity, current KV segment set, and stale/replica allowance.
- KV segmentation: partition the KV address space into many small, power-of-two segments (e.g., 256–1024 segments per model) instead of a few large shards. Each GPU owns a set of segments. Segments are replicated at low replication factor (r=1 or 2) depending on criticality. Replication is warm but lazy: a primary owner holds authoritative writes; secondaries pull diffs or only keep read-only copies of stable prefixes.
- Elastic routing uses a lightweight consistent-hash + cost model: for an incoming request we compute token-prefix fingerprints to estimate likely KV segment hotness and route to the GPU whose segments match the hot prefix set to maximize local KV hits. When no single GPU has enough of the hot segments, requests are routed to a GPU-group and we schedule intra-request sub-ops (see "hybrid execution" below).

Key components:
1) Segment registry: a small metadata service (distributed, highly available) that maps segment -> owner list, last-update-timestamp, and staleness policy. This registry is cacheable on serving nodes and refreshed on TTL.

2) Router (per-node): computes a cost for executing the request locally vs remote fetches. Cost factors: local KV hit ratio estimate, estimated NCCL cost if we require multi-GPU collectives, current GPU queue length, and network RTT to other GPU nodes. Router produces: prefer-local (single GPU), prefer-group (2–3 GPUs with overlapping segments), or prefer-fallback (smaller model variant).

3) Hybrid execution mode: when a request requires many segments across GPUs, instead of a heavy synchronous NCCL across all GPUs per token, we split the request into pipeline stages: attention compute for tokens served by GPU A proceeds and flushes partial KV writes into a small per-segment delta log; GPUs that need those deltas either subscribe or pull them asynchronously. For cross-GPU attention where exact ordering matters, we fall back to an ordered handshake among a small set of GPUs (bounded by a tunable fanout). This reduces global NCCL frequency and keeps collectives local and smaller.

4) Segment migration and balancing: background balancer monitors segment hotness (access counts in sliding windows) and migrates hot segments towards GPUs with spare compute capacity. Migration uses "copy-on-write" semantics: new owner starts as read-replica, pulls current segment snapshot, then becomes primary after a short quiesce. Writes during migration are appended to a delta log and reconciled on takeover. This keeps migration bandwidth small and bounded.

NCCL tuning notes (practical heuristics we've prototyped):
- Avoid global allreduce for KV presence checks. Instead, rely on local caches + small RPC probes to known owners when local miss occurs.
- For collective ops that remain (e.g., KV broadcast for model-level state), prefer hierarchical collectives: within-rack NCCL collectives then cross-rack via ring-of-rings. This reduces RDMA pressure.
- Use NCCL LL/LL128 where supported for intra-node gradients-like ops; but for our per-token small KV transfers, NCCL launch overhead dominates. In those cases, prefer batched RPCs over NCCL if fanout>4.

Compatibility with tensor/pipeline parallelism:
- This design assumes model weights are either replicated across GPUs (data-parallel or model-sharded with weight-aware routing) or partitioned but co-located with KV segment ownership. For tensor-parallel models we need a lightweight mapping layer that binds KV segments to the tensor-slab owners so that attention compute and KV access remain co-located. That mapping is part of the segment registry and is updated when model placement changes.

Instrumentation and metrics:
- Per-request: estimated local-KV-hit-ratio, actual local-KV-hit-ratio, number of remote segment fetches, NCCL-call-count, NCCL-bytes, per-token latency (p50/p95/p99), fallback usage.
- Per-segment: access-rate, average token-offset distribution, replication-count, last-migration-time, migration-bandwidth.
- Balancer: rebalancing-rate, bandwidth-used, migration-failure-rate.

Experiment plan (short term):
1) Microbench: synthetic workload with controlled prefix distributions; compare static big-shards vs many-small-segments with elastic router. Metrics: p99 token latency, NCCL ops per second, remote-fetch rate.
2) Real traffic replay: sample 2 weeks of production queries (anonymized) and replay across both systems. Measure end-to-end tail latency and cross-GPU network bytes.
3) Stress test: scale cluster from 4->32 GPUs and measure migration times and latency spikes during up/down events.

Operational considerations and failure modes:
- Registry partition loss: router must be able to operate with cached mapping for a TTL and fall back to conservative routing (prefer-group).
- Split-brain around ownership during simultaneous migrations: ensure delta-logs have monotonically increasing sequence numbers and that takeover requires quorum acknowledgement (design uses simple leader lease).
- Cold-start of segments: when a new model version loads, initial segment population can be bandwidth-heavy. Plan: adopt lazy population + small prioritized prefetch (hot segments first).

Open questions / tradeoffs to discuss in review:
- Segment granularity sweet spot (256 vs 1024 segments) — tradeoff between metadata size, routing decision cost, and migration granularity.
- Replication factor: r=1 minimizes memory but raises cross-GPU fetches on misses. r=2 reduces misses but increases memory and sync complexity.
- When is NCCL still the right tool vs custom RPC? Fanout threshold? operation size threshold?
- Consistency model for KV writes during streaming generation (strict vs last-writer-wins) — we currently prefer primary authoritative with ordered deltas, but performance impact needs measurement.

Next steps (actionable):
- Jamal: implement a lightweight segment registry prototype (thin HTTP API + in-memory snapshot cache) — due 2025-02-21.
- Priya: build the router cost model stub and synthetic workload harness — due 2025-02-28.
- Aisha (owner): run initial microbench comparisons and write measured results in this doc — target 2025-03-14.
- Team sync: prioritize a design review with serving-runtime and infra (slot on 2025-03-03).

Notes to self / rough thoughts (informal):
- This feels like a middle ground between full sharding and full replication: we get locality for hot prefixes and graceful elastic scaling.
- Might be able to reuse parts of the existing routing/fallback code in the hosted API; router is intentionally small and policy-driven.
- Keep early implementation in a non-blocking path so we can A/B test with small percentage of traffic.

References and background reading (internal):
- previous experiments: ENG-7632 (small-shard tradeoffs), PR#623 (kv delta logs), notes from "nccl-batching" thread in #serving-runtime Slack.

End of draft.
